title: Kafka
subtitle: 32 questions covering all key topics · Shuffled each attempt

questions.q: What is a Kafka partition?
opts: A logical grouping of topics that share a common producer
An ordered, immutable sequence of messages that is continually appended to — like an append-only log file
A physical server in the Kafka cluster responsible for storing all data
A consumer group assignment that maps topics to individual consumers
questions.expl: A partition is an ordered, immutable sequence of messages continuously appended to — essentially a log file. Partitions are how Kafka scales: they allow messages to be consumed in parallel and distributed across brokers.

questions.q: What is the difference between a topic and a partition in Kafka?
opts: Topics store messages; partitions store metadata about those messages
A topic is a logical grouping of messages; a partition is the physical grouping — a topic can span multiple partitions across different brokers
Topics are for producers; partitions are for consumers
Topics are replicated; partitions are not
questions.expl: A topic is a logical grouping of messages — how you organize and subscribe to data. A partition is the physical unit — an actual log file on a broker. A single topic can have many partitions spread across many brokers, enabling parallel consumption and horizontal scaling.

questions.q: What is a Kafka broker?
opts: A client library that helps producers serialize messages before sending
An individual server (physical or virtual) responsible for storing data and serving clients
The coordination service that manages leader election across the cluster
A routing layer that sits between producers and partitions
questions.expl: A broker is simply an individual server in the Kafka cluster. Each broker stores data (partitions) and serves clients (producers and consumers). Adding more brokers increases both storage capacity and the number of clients you can serve.

questions.q: What are the four fields of a Kafka message/record?
opts: Topic, partition, offset, and checksum
Value (payload), key, timestamp, and headers
Producer ID, consumer ID, sequence number, and payload
Topic, key, value, and replication factor
questions.expl: A Kafka record has four fields, all technically optional: value (the payload), key (used to determine partition routing), timestamp (when the message was created or ingested), and headers (key-value metadata pairs, like HTTP headers).

questions.q: What is an offset in Kafka?
opts: The number of bytes between the start of a partition and the current message
A unique sequential identifier assigned to each message within a partition, used by consumers to track their reading progress
The lag between when a message is produced and when it is consumed
The position of a partition's leader replica within the broker cluster
questions.expl: Each message in a partition gets a unique offset — a sequential ID indicating its position. Consumers use offsets to track progress. When a consumer restarts, it reads its last committed offset and resumes from there. Ordering within a partition is determined by offsets, not timestamps.

questions.q: How does Kafka determine which partition a message goes to when a key is provided?
opts: The producer manually specifies the partition number in the message headers
Kafka hashes the key (using murmur2 by default) and takes the modulo with the number of partitions: partition = hash(key) % num_partitions
Kafka assigns partitions round-robin regardless of the key
The broker cluster controller assigns partitions based on current load
questions.expl: When a key is provided, Kafka hashes it using murmur2 by default and computes partition = hash(key) % num_partitions. Messages with the same key always go to the same partition, which is what preserves ordering for related messages.

questions.q: What happens when a Kafka message is sent without a key?
opts: The message is rejected — keys are required for Kafka to function
Modern Kafka clients use a 'sticky' partitioner that batches to one partition for efficiency, then rotates — producing roughly even distribution over time but losing ordering guarantees
The message is broadcast to all partitions simultaneously
Kafka assigns it to partition 0 by default
questions.expl: Without a key, modern Kafka clients use a sticky partitioner — batching messages to one partition for efficiency before rotating to the next. This produces roughly even distribution over time but loses the ability to guarantee ordering for related messages since they may land on different partitions.

questions.q: Why is the choice of partition key so critical in system design?
opts: A bad key increases message size, hurting throughput
A bad key creates hot partitions — some partitions get overwhelmed with traffic while others sit idle, negating the benefits of distribution
A bad key prevents consumers from committing offsets correctly
A bad key forces Kafka to use replication factor 1, reducing durability
questions.expl: The partition key determines how load is distributed. A poorly chosen key causes hot partitions — one partition receiving far more traffic than others. Good keys distribute messages evenly across the partition space. The article calls partitioning strategy 'the main decision you make when dealing with Kafka clusters.'

questions.q: An Ad Click Aggregator partitions by ad_id. Nike launches a viral Lebron James ad. What problem occurs and what are two ways to fix it?
opts: The partition for that ad_id runs out of disk space; fix by increasing retention.bytes or adding a new broker
A hot partition forms because all clicks for that ad hit one partition; fix with random salting (add a random suffix to the key) or a compound key (ad_id + region or user segment)
The consumer group loses track of offsets for that ad; fix by resetting offsets or using a dead letter queue
Replication falls behind because the leader is overwhelmed; fix by increasing the replication factor
questions.expl: All clicks for the viral ad hash to the same partition, creating a hot partition. Two fixes: (1) Random salting — append a random number to the ad_id so clicks spread across multiple partitions (complicates aggregation); (2) Compound key — use ad_id + region or user_segment to distribute load while preserving some grouping.

questions.q: How does a Kafka consumer group ensure each message is processed by only one consumer?
opts: Each consumer in the group maintains a lock on the messages it's reading
Each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group — so messages in a partition are processed by only one consumer at a time
The broker tracks which messages have been delivered and prevents re-delivery to other consumers in the group
Consumer groups use a coordinator node that routes each message to an available consumer
questions.expl: In a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer. Since messages within a partition are consumed by one consumer, each message is effectively processed once under normal operation. If a consumer fails, Kafka rebalances and redistributes its partitions to remaining consumers.

questions.q: What happens to partitions when a consumer in a group fails?
opts: The failed consumer's partitions are paused until it restarts
Kafka rebalances the consumer group, redistributing the failed consumer's partitions among the remaining active consumers
The partition leader broker temporarily takes over processing for the failed consumer
The messages in the failed consumer's partitions are moved to a dead letter queue
questions.expl: When a consumer in a group fails, Kafka triggers a rebalance. The failed consumer's partitions are redistributed among the remaining consumers in the group, ensuring all partitions continue to be processed. The new consumer picks up from the last committed offset.

questions.q: What is the maximum useful number of consumers in a consumer group for a topic with N partitions?
opts: Unlimited — Kafka can distribute one partition to multiple consumers simultaneously
N consumers — adding more than N consumers means some consumers sit idle since each partition is assigned to at most one consumer
N/2 consumers — Kafka reserves half the consumer slots for failover
2N consumers — Kafka assigns each partition to a primary and backup consumer
questions.expl: Since each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in a group, having more consumers than partitions means the extra consumers sit idle — they have no partitions to read from. The maximum parallelism is equal to the number of partitions. This is why adding partitions is how you scale consumer throughput.

questions.q: What delivery guarantee does Kafka provide by default, and what causes it?
opts: Exactly-once — Kafka deduplicates all messages automatically
At-least-once — if a consumer crashes after processing a message but before committing its offset, the message will be reprocessed after restart
At-most-once — messages are acknowledged before processing to avoid duplicates
Best-effort — Kafka makes no delivery guarantees without additional configuration
questions.expl: Kafka's default is at-least-once delivery. If a consumer processes a message and then crashes before committing its offset, Kafka will re-deliver that message after restart (the consumer resumes from the last committed offset). Exactly-once semantics are possible but require additional configuration: idempotent producers + transactional APIs.

questions.q: What does setting acks=all on a Kafka producer do?
opts: The producer waits for all consumers to acknowledge they've processed the message
The message is acknowledged only when all in-sync replicas (ISR) have received it — the strongest durability guarantee available
The message is sent to all brokers simultaneously rather than just the partition leader
The producer receives acknowledgment from the controller rather than the partition leader
questions.expl: acks=all means the leader only acknowledges the write after all in-sync replicas (ISR) have also received it. This is the strongest durability guarantee — even if the leader immediately fails after acknowledging, the data exists on all in-sync replicas and won't be lost.

questions.q: When should you commit a consumer offset, and what is the tradeoff?
opts: Always commit immediately upon receiving a message to minimize reprocessing
Commit only after the work associated with the message is fully complete — the more work done per message, the more reprocessing risk if the consumer fails before committing
Commit offsets on a fixed timer (every 5 seconds) regardless of processing status
Never commit offsets manually — Kafka auto-commits after every poll
questions.expl: Committing before work is done risks losing the message (at-most-once). Committing after work completes risks reprocessing (at-least-once). The article uses Design a Web Crawler as an example: don't commit the offset until raw HTML is safely stored in S3. More work per message = more reprocessing risk on failure, so keeping consumer work small is a good strategy.

questions.q: How does Kafka's leader-follower replication model work?
opts: All brokers receive writes simultaneously; the fastest acknowledgment wins
Each partition has one leader replica that handles all writes; follower replicas passively replicate from the leader. If the leader fails, the controller promotes an in-sync follower
Producers write to follower replicas first; the controller forwards to the leader after quorum
Leaders and followers alternate roles on a rotating schedule to distribute write load
questions.expl: Each partition has a single leader replica that handles all writes (and reads by default). Followers passively replicate from the leader, staying in sync. When a leader fails, the cluster controller promotes one of the in-sync follower replicas to leader, minimizing downtime and data loss.

questions.q: What is a replication factor of 3 in Kafka and what does it protect against?
opts: 3 copies of each topic (not partition) are maintained across brokers

Each partition has 3 total replicas (1 leader + 2 followers) on different brokers — the data remains available if one broker fails, and can survive a second broker failure if the remaining in-sync replica is promoted
Each message is written 3 times to the same partition for redundancy
3 consumer groups can independently read each partition simultaneously
questions.expl: A replication factor of 3 means each partition has 3 copies across 3 different brokers. If one broker fails, 2 copies remain. A common configuration: 1 leader + 2 followers per partition. The cluster can survive a broker failure with no data loss and no interruption (a follower is promoted to leader).

questions.q: The article says 'Kafka is always available, sometimes consistent.' What does this mean in an interview context?
opts: Kafka guarantees availability over consistency, meaning reads may return stale data during network partitions
It's not realistic to ask 'what if Kafka goes down' — Kafka itself is highly available. The more relevant failure scenario is a consumer going down, and you should design around that
Kafka uses eventual consistency for replication, so follower replicas may lag the leader
Kafka prioritizes write availability over read consistency during broker failures
questions.expl: The article explicitly says asking 'what happens if Kafka goes down?' is unrealistic and you can gently push back on interviewers who ask it. The far more relevant and likely failure is a consumer going down. Design around consumer failures: offset management, rebalancing, retry topics, and DLQs.

questions.q: What is the key difference between using Kafka as a message queue vs. as a stream?
opts: Message queues use topics; streams use partitions directly

As a message queue, each message is processed by one consumer in a group and effectively consumed. As a stream, the log is retained and can be replayed, multiple independent consumer groups can read the same data, and processing is continuous
Message queues delete messages after consumption; streams compress messages instead
Message queues support ordering; streams do not
questions.expl: Both modes use offset commits for tracking. The difference is consumption pattern: as a queue, one consumer group processes each message and moves on (though Kafka retains based on retention policy). As a stream, the log is retained for replay, multiple independent consumer groups can read the same data at their own pace, and processing is continuous.

questions.q: Which of these use cases best fits Kafka as a message queue (vs. a stream)?
opts: Aggregating ad click events in real-time to compute click-through rates
Ensuring users enter a concert ticket booking page in the order they arrived — a virtual waiting queue
Sending the same event to multiple independent analytics systems simultaneously
Allowing multiple consumer groups to replay historical data for different purposes
questions.expl: A virtual waiting queue for Ticketmaster is a classic message queue use case: each user event should be processed by exactly one consumer, in order, exactly once. Stream use cases (ad click aggregation, fan-out to multiple consumers, replay) involve continuous processing or multiple independent consumers reading the same data.

questions.q: What is a rough estimate for a single Kafka broker's throughput and storage capacity?
opts: ~10K messages/second and ~100GB storage
~1M messages/second and ~1TB storage (varies significantly with message size and hardware)
~100K messages/second and ~10TB storage
~10M messages/second and ~100TB storage
questions.expl: On good hardware, a single broker can handle around 1M messages/second and store around 1TB of data. These are rough estimates that depend heavily on message size and hardware specs, but they're useful for estimating in an interview whether scaling is even a concern for your design.

questions.q: When adding brokers to scale Kafka, what else must you ensure?
opts: You must increase acks settings to account for the additional brokers
Your topics must have sufficient partitions to take advantage of the new brokers — under-partitioned topics can't distribute load across new brokers
You must restart all consumers to trigger rebalancing across the new brokers
You must reconfigure all producer keys to include the new broker addresses
questions.expl: Adding brokers without enough partitions means the new brokers sit underutilized. Partitions are the unit of parallelism in Kafka — if you have 3 brokers but only 3 partitions, adding a 4th broker gains you nothing until you also increase the number of partitions. More partitions enable more parallelism and better load distribution.

questions.q: What is the anti-pattern of storing large blobs in Kafka, and what is the correct approach?
opts: Large blobs slow down consumer offset commits; instead split them into smaller chunks
Kafka isn't meant to store large files — store the file in a distributed system like S3 and put a small pointer message (the S3 location) in Kafka instead
Large blobs should be stored in a separate Kafka topic with higher retention
Compress large blobs with GZIP before sending to Kafka to keep message size manageable
questions.expl: Kafka is designed for small messages processed quickly, not large file storage. A common anti-pattern is putting videos in Kafka for transcoding workers. The correct approach: store the video in S3, put a small Kafka message containing the S3 URL. The message is tiny and serves as a pointer. This avoids memory pressure, poor network utilization, and throughput degradation.

questions.q: Why should you enable idempotent producer mode when using retries?
opts: Idempotent mode compresses retry messages to reduce network overhead
Without idempotent mode, a retry after a network timeout can result in duplicate messages if the original message was actually received; idempotent mode ensures each message is written exactly once
Idempotent mode allows retries to target different partitions if the original partition is unavailable
Idempotent mode enables the producer to verify message integrity using checksums
questions.expl: When a producer retries a message (e.g., after a network timeout), it's possible the original message was received but the acknowledgment was lost. Without idempotent mode, the retry creates a duplicate. Idempotent mode assigns each message a sequence number so Kafka can detect and discard duplicates, giving you exactly-once writes at the producer level.

questions.q: How does Kafka handle consumer-side retries, since Kafka doesn't support them out of the box?
opts: Kafka supports consumer retries via the retry.backoff.ms configuration on the consumer
Failed messages are moved to a retry topic; a separate consumer processes retries and eventually moves messages to a dead letter queue (DLQ) after too many failures
Consumers re-seek to the failed offset automatically after a configurable timeout
The consumer group coordinator handles retries by reassigning failed messages to another consumer
questions.expl: Unlike SQS, Kafka doesn't support consumer retries natively. The common pattern: when a message fails processing, publish it to a retry topic. A separate consumer processes the retry topic. After a maximum number of retries, move the message to a dead letter queue (DLQ) for investigation. This is why the article notes they chose SQS over Kafka for Design a Web Crawler — to get built-in retry and DLQ support.

questions.q: What is a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) in Kafka?
opts: A Kafka topic with infinite retention used as the primary data store
A topic where messages that have failed processing too many times are stored for later investigation
A special partition that receives messages when the consumer group rebalances
A Kafka log compaction topic that retains only the latest value per key
questions.expl: A DLQ is a topic where messages that have exhausted their retries are sent instead of being dropped or blocking the main consumer. It allows operators to inspect failed messages, understand why they failed, and decide whether to replay them or discard them — without blocking the main processing pipeline.

questions.q: What are two built-in ways to improve Kafka producer throughput?
opts: Increasing replication factor and enabling rack-aware assignment
Batching multiple messages in a single send() call and enabling message compression (GZIP, Snappy, LZ4) to reduce message size
Using sticky partitioner and increasing consumer group size
Enabling acks=0 and increasing max.poll.records on consumers
questions.expl: Two key producer throughput optimizations: (1) Batching — send multiple messages in one send() call to reduce network overhead (Kafka producers naturally batch before sending); (2) Compression — GZIP, Snappy, or LZ4 reduce message size, allowing more data per network round trip. The article also notes that partitioning strategy is arguably the biggest performance lever.

questions.q: What is the recommended maximum message size in Kafka and why?
opts: Under 10KB — Kafka's network protocol has overhead that makes larger messages inefficient
Under 1MB — to ensure optimal performance via reduced memory pressure and better network utilization
Under 10MB — the default broker configuration rejects larger messages
Under 100KB — to stay within a single partition page for efficient reads
questions.expl: The article recommends keeping messages under 1MB for optimal performance. While message.max.bytes is configurable, large messages increase memory pressure, hurt network utilization, and slow throughput. Large data (like videos) should be stored externally (S3) with only a pointer in Kafka.

questions.q: Which scenario is best suited for Kafka as an asynchronous message queue?
opts: Aggregating real-time sensor readings for a live dashboard that must reflect data within 100ms
Processing video transcoding after upload — make the standard definition video available immediately and queue the transcoding job asynchronously
Synchronizing database writes across multiple shards with exactly-once guarantees
Serving user profile reads with low latency at high throughput
questions.expl: Video transcoding is the canonical async queue use case from the article: make the SD video immediately available, then put a message in Kafka with the video's S3 location for the transcoding worker to pick up asynchronously when capacity is available. The producer (upload service) and consumer (transcoder) are decoupled and scale independently.

questions.q: When should you choose SQS over Kafka?
opts: When you need to process more than 1M messages per second
When you want built-in retry logic and dead letter queue support without implementing it yourself
When you need strict message ordering across multiple partitions
When you need multiple consumer groups to read the same messages independently
questions.expl: SQS provides built-in retry and DLQ functionality that Kafka lacks natively. The article explicitly notes this tradeoff in Design a Web Crawler: they chose SQS over Kafka specifically to avoid implementing custom retry and DLQ logic. If you need simple queue semantics with built-in failure handling, SQS is often simpler than Kafka.

questions.q: What should be the FIRST topic you discuss in an interview when scaling a Kafka-based system?
opts: Replication factor and acks settings for durability
Partitioning strategy — how you'll partition data and how you'll handle hot partitions
Number of brokers to add and how to distribute them across availability zones
Consumer group configuration and offset commit strategy
questions.expl: The article is explicit: 'discussing the partition strategy should just about always be where you start.' Partitioning is the main architectural decision in Kafka — it determines how load is distributed, whether ordering is preserved, and whether hot partitions will be a problem. Everything else (broker count, consumer scaling) follows from getting partitioning right.

questions.q: What is Kafka's default message retention period and how is it configured?
opts: 24 hours, configured via retention.hours
7 days, configured via retention.ms and retention.bytes settings on the topic
30 days, configured via log.retention.days in the broker config
Indefinite by default — messages are only removed by explicit deletion
questions.expl: Kafka's default retention policy keeps messages for 7 days. This is configured via retention.ms (time-based) and retention.bytes (size-based) settings per topic. In an interview, if you need longer retention for replay or auditing, you can increase these settings — just account for the storage cost impact.

questions.q: Why is Kafka described as a 'distributed commit log'?
opts: Because it uses a write-ahead log internally for crash recovery
Because each partition is an append-only log — messages are written sequentially and assigned offsets, and once written they're never modified in-place
Because producers must commit a transaction log before messages are visible to consumers
Because the controller logs all cluster metadata changes to a central commit log
questions.expl: Kafka is called a distributed commit log because each partition functions as an append-only, ordered, immutable log. Messages are sequentially appended and assigned offsets. They're never modified in-place — only eventually removed by retention policies or log compaction. This immutability is central to Kafka's performance, reliability, and replication simplicity.
